catalog_quote: [Eades 1976:25, as carried by StressTyp2] Most words have initial main stress. Some words have primary stress on the second syllable; most of these words have a long vowel in the second syllable. There is no secondary stress.. Dharrawal, from archival transcriptions] Stress falls on the first syllable in disyllabic words and no example is found in the source material that shows stress on the final syllable in a disyllabic word.. In words with three syllables or more, primary stress falls on the first or second syllable. Where stress is marked on a second syllable in a polysyllabic word, a long vowel in that stressed syllable is in some cases indicated.. audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-hedged: initial default, some peninitial stress mostly on long vowels, no secondary stress) rests on Eades 1976:25-26, the sole audio-based sketch of this no-longer-spoken language, but we hold only StressTyp2's carry of that passage, confirmed verbatim in the held bundle (passage 878). The supporting Besold 2012 PhD (pp.113-114) is held and its quoted sentences are confirmed verbatim; it independently agrees (initial stress; second-syllable stress in polysyllables sometimes with a marked long vowel; length and stress independent in some Mathews forms), so nothing suggests the hedged coding is wrong. Glottolog's four descriptive refs contain nothing better; Mathews 1901 (downloaded now, public domain) has no stress statement. No instrumental or modern phonology study exists.
